claims.evidence: This is supported by structural comparison with published structures.

claims.claim: The RVxF sequence LIRF(519-522) is critical for Phactr1/PP1 complex formation.
claims.source: The RVxF sequence LIRF(519-522) is critical for Phactr1/PP1 complex formation (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A). Its deletion decreased binding affinity ~104 fold, while the I520A and F522A mutations reduced it 4-fold and ~650 fold respectively (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis and binding affinity data.

claims.claim: Deletion of the LIRF sequence decreased Phactr1-PP1 binding affinity ~104 fold.
claims.source: Its deletion decreased binding affinity ~104 fold, while the I520A and F522A mutations reduced it 4-fold and ~650 fold respectively (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Bio-layer interferometry data.

claims.claim: The I520A mutation reduced Phactr1-PP1 binding affinity 4-fold.
claims.source: Its deletion decreased binding affinity ~104 fold, while the I520A and F522A mutations reduced it 4-fold and ~650 fold respectively (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Bio-layer interferometry data.

claims.claim: The F522A mutation reduced Phactr1-PP1 binding affinity ~650 fold.
claims.source: Its deletion decreased binding affinity ~104 fold, while the I520A and F522A mutations reduced it 4-fold and ~650 fold respectively (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Bio-layer interferometry data.

claims.claim: The RVxF residue L519 makes contacts with G-actin in the trivalent G-actin•Phactr1 RPEL domain complex.
claims.source: The RVxF residue L519 also makes contacts with G-actin in the trivalent G-actin•Phactr1 RPEL domain complex (Mouilleron et al., 2012), explaining why PP1 and G-actin binding to Phactr proteins is mutually exclusive (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B; Wiezlak et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by structural data from Mouilleron et al., 2012.

claims.claim: PP1 and G-actin binding to Phactr proteins is mutually exclusive.
claims.source: The RVxF residue L519 also makes contacts with G-actin in the trivalent G-actin•Phactr1 RPEL domain complex (Mouilleron et al., 2012), explaining why PP1 and G-actin binding to Phactr proteins is mutually exclusive (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B; Wiezlak et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by structural analysis and citation to Wiezlak et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Substitution of R536 by proline reduced Phactr1-binding affinity >300 fold.
claims.source: Substitution of R536 by proline, as in the mouse Phactr4 'humdy' mutation (Kim et al., 2007), reduced Phactr1-binding affinity >300 fold, while Y534A reduced it > 10 fold (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Bio-layer interferometry data.

claims.claim: The Y534A mutation reduced Phactr1-PP1 binding affinity > 10 fold.
claims.source: Substitution of R536 by proline, as in the mouse Phactr4 'humdy' mutation (Kim et al., 2007), reduced Phactr1-binding affinity >300 fold, while Y534A reduced it > 10 fold (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Bio-layer interferometry data.

claims.claim: The W542A mutation reduced PP1-binding affinity ~40-fold.
claims.source: Although W542A reduced PP1-binding affinity ~40-fold, R544A reduced it ~ threefold (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Bio-layer interferometry data.

claims.claim: The R544A mutation reduced PP1-binding affinity ~ threefold.
claims.source: Although W542A reduced PP1-binding affinity ~40-fold, R544A reduced it ~ threefold (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Bio-layer interferometry data.

claims.claim: Phactr1 residues 545–565 include a five-turn amphipathic α-helix that abuts the PP1 hydrophobic groove.
claims.source: Residues 545–565 include a five-turn amphipathic α-helix that abuts the PP1 hydrophobic groove: Phactr1 residues L545, I553, L557, F560 make hydrophobic contacts with PP1 I133, R132, W149, and K150, while E556 and E564 make salt bridges with PP1 R132 and K150, respectively, and K561 hydrogen bonds with PP1 S129 and D194 (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by structural analysis of the crystal structure.

claims.claim: A triple alanine substitution of Phactr1 L557, F560 and L574 (LFL-3A) resulted in a ~ 900 fold drop in binding affinity.
claims.source: A triple alanine substitution of Phactr1 L557, F560 and L574 (LFL-3A) resulted in a ~ 900 fold drop in binding affinity, while the acidic substitution L574D reduced binding affinity by 17-fold.
claims.evidence: This is supported by Bio-layer interferometry data.

claims.claim: The L574D mutation reduced Phactr1-PP1 binding affinity by 17-fold.
claims.source: A triple alanine substitution of Phactr1 L557, F560 and L574 (LFL-3A) resulted in a ~ 900 fold drop in binding affinity, while the acidic substitution L574D reduced binding affinity by 17-fold.
claims.evidence: This is supported by Bio-layer interferometry data.

claims.claim: The F577A mutation reduced Phactr1-PP1 binding activity by 16-fold.
claims.source: Mutations F577A and H578A reduced binding activity by 16-fold and 7-fold, respectively, corroborating previous co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Allen et al., 2004; Sagara et al., 2009), and mutation of all three C-terminal histidines (HHH-A) reduced affinity >50 fold (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Bio-layer interferometry data.

claims.claim: The H578A mutation reduced Phactr1-PP1 binding activity by 7-fold.
claims.source: Mutations F577A and H578A reduced binding activity by 16-fold and 7-fold, respectively, corroborating previous co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Allen et al., 2004; Sagara et al., 2009), and mutation of all three C-terminal histidines (HHH-A) reduced affinity >50 fold (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Bio-layer interferometry data.

claims.claim: Mutation of all three C-terminal histidines (HHH-A) reduced Phactr1-PP1 affinity >50 fold.
claims.source: Mutations F577A and H578A reduced binding activity by 16-fold and 7-fold, respectively, corroborating previous co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Allen et al., 2004; Sagara et al., 2009), and mutation of all three C-terminal histidines (HHH-A) reduced affinity >50 fold (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Bio-layer interferometry data.

claims.claim: The docking of Phactr1 C-terminal sequences across the PP1 hydrophobic groove substantially modifies its topography.
claims.source: The docking of Phactr1 C-terminal sequences across the PP1 hydrophobic groove substantially modifies its topography (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by structural analysis of the crystal structure.

claims.claim: The positioning of the Phactr1 amphipathic helix creates a deep hydrophobic pocket comprising Phactr1 W542, L545, K550, I553, R554, L557 and H578, and PP1 I130 I133 and Y134.
claims.source: The positioning of the Phactr1 amphipathic helix creates a deep hydrophobic pocket comprising Phactr1 W542, L545, K550, I553, R554, L557 and H578, and PP1 I130 I133 and Y134.
claims.evidence: This is supported by structural analysis of the crystal structure.

claims.claim: A narrow amphipathic cavity is formed by the positioning of Phactr1 K561 and R576 across the PP1 hydrophobic groove.
claims.source: Adjacent to the pocket, a narrow amphipathic cavity is formed by the positioning of Phactr1 K561 and R576 across the PP1 hydrophobic groove: its polar side comprises Phactr1 K561 and R576, and PP1 D194 and S129, while its hydrophobic side is formed from PP1 residues C127, I130, V195, W206 and V223.
claims.evidence: This is supported by structural analysis of the crystal structure.

claims.claim: Three water molecules and a glycerol are resolved within the amphipathic cavity.
claims.source: Three water molecules and a glycerol are resolved within the cavity, whose hydrophobic side forms part of the binding site for the PP1 inhibitors tautomycetin and tautomycin (Choy et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by structural analysis of the crystal structure.

claims.claim: The hydrophobic side of the amphipathic cavity forms part of the binding site for the PP1 inhibitors tautomycetin and tautomycin.
claims.source: Three water molecules and a glycerol are resolved within the cavity, whose hydrophobic side forms part of the binding site for the PP1 inhibitors tautomycetin and tautomycin (Choy et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison with published structures from Choy et al., 2017.

claims.claim: A basic rim is formed from Phactr1 residues K550, R554, R576, H578 and R579.
claims.source: The new composite surface is crowned by a basic rim, formed from Phactr1 residues K550, R554, R576, H578 and R579 (Figure 2B), which radically alters the surface charge distribution (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by structural analysis of the crystal structure.

claims.claim: Phactr1 binding radically alters the PP1 surface charge distribution.
claims.source: The new composite surface is crowned by a basic rim, formed from Phactr1 residues K550, R554, R576, H578 and R579 (Figure 2B), which radically alters the surface charge distribution (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by structural analysis and electrostatic surface potential calculations.

claims.claim: Phactr1 binding transforms the surface of PP1 adjacent to its catalytic site in a way distinct from that seen in the spinophilin/PP1 complex.
claims.source: Thus, Phactr1 binding profoundly transforms the surface of PP1 adjacent to its catalytic site. This transformation is distinct from that seen in the spinophilin/PP1 complex (Ragusa et al., 2010), which modifies the hydrophobic groove in a different way and leaves the PP1 surface electrostatics unchanged (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by structural comparison with the spinophilin/PP1 complex.

claims.claim: Expression of Phactr1XXX induces F-actin rearrangements in NIH3T3 fibroblasts, provided it can bind PP1.
claims.source: We previously showed that expression of an activated Phactr1 derivative that constitutively forms the Phactr1/PP1 complex, Phactr1XXX, induces F-actin rearrangements in NIH3T3 fibroblasts, provided it can bind PP1 (Wiezlak et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wiezlak et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Overexpression of the Phactr1 PP1-binding domain alone can induce cytoskeletal changes.
claims.source: Indeed, overexpression of the Phactr1 PP1-binding domain alone can also induce such changes, suggesting that the Phactr1 C-terminal sequences are sufficient to allow recognition of at least some substrates (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A; see Discussion).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Over 3000 phosphorylation sites were quantified in the SILAC phosphoproteomics experiment.
claims.source: Over 3000 phosphorylation sites were quantified, and each assigned a dephosphorylation score comparing their phosphorylation with that observed in cells inducibly expressing Phactr1XXXΔC, which lacks the PP1 binding sequences, or vector alone (Figure 3A; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, Supplementary file 1, Table A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the SILAC phosphoproteomics data.

claims.claim: Annotation enrichment analysis identified 'regulation of actin filament-based process' and 'regulation of actin cytoskeleton organisation' as categories with significantly higher mean dephosphorylation score upon expression of Phactr1XXX.
claims.source: Annotation enrichment analysis of the whole dataset (Cox and Mann, 2012) identified two Gene Ontology Biological Process categories that exhibited a significantly higher mean dephosphorylation score upon expression of Phactr1XXX: 'regulation of actin filament-based process' and 'regulation of actin cytoskeleton organisation' (Figure 3B, Supplementary file 1, Table B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by annotation enrichment analysis of the phosphoproteomics data.

claims.claim: Proteins with a high dephosphorylation score included many cytoskeletal components and regulators.
claims.source: In keeping with this, proteins with a high dephosphorylation score included many cytoskeletal components and regulators (Figure 3C, Supplementary file 1, Table A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the SILAC phosphoproteomics data.

claims.claim: Sites with dephosphorylation scores > 2.5 were enriched in acidic residues at positions +2 to +7 relative to the phosphorylation site, with small hydrophobic residues enriched at positions +4 and +5, and basic residues N-terminal to it.
claims.source: Proline-directed sites predominated in the dataset as a whole, but those sites with dephosphorylation scores > 2.5 were enriched in acidic residues at positions +2 to +7 relative to the phosphorylation site, with small hydrophobic residues enriched at positions +4 and +5, and basic residues N-terminal to it (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis of the phosphoproteomics data.

claims.claim: IRSp53 pS455 exhibited a low KM and high kcat/KM in the in vitro peptide dephosphorylation assay.
claims.source: Synthetic phosphopeptides containing the candidate sites exhibited a range of KM and kcat/KM values: for example, IRSp53 pS455 exhibited a low KM and high kcat/KM; spectrin αII pS1031 had a similar KM but lower kcat/KM; and afadin pS1275 was as reactive as spectrin αII pS1031, but with much poorer KM (Figure 3C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C; Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by in vitro phosphatase assay data.

claims.claim: Spectrin αII pS1031 had a similar KM to IRSp53 pS455 but lower kcat/KM.
claims.source: Synthetic phosphopeptides containing the candidate sites exhibited a range of KM and kcat/KM values: for example, IRSp53 pS455 exhibited a low KM and high kcat/KM; spectrin αII pS1031 had a similar KM but lower kcat/KM; and afadin pS1275 was as reactive as spectrin αII pS1031, but with much poorer KM (Figure 3C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C; Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by in vitro phosphatase assay data.

claims.claim: Afadin pS1275 was as reactive as spectrin αII pS1031, but with much poorer KM.
claims.source: Synthetic phosphopeptides containing the candidate sites exhibited a range of KM and kcat/KM values: for example, IRSp53 pS455 exhibited a low KM and high kcat/KM; spectrin αII pS1031 had a similar KM but lower kcat/KM; and afadin pS1275 was as reactive as spectrin αII pS1031, but with much poorer KM (Figure 3C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C; Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by in vitro phosphatase assay data.

claims.claim: The four substrates with the lowest KM all contained a leucine doublet at the +4 and +5 positions.
claims.source: Interestingly, the four substrates with the lowest KM - IRSp53 pS455, Plekho2 pS395, spectrin αII pS1031, and Tbc1d15 pS205 - all contained a leucine doublet at the +4 and +5 positions (see Discussion).
claims.evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis and kinetic data.

claims.claim: Phosphorylation of IRSp53 S455 and afadin S1275 was substantially decreased upon expression of Phactr1XXX in NIH3T3 cells.
claims.source: Immunoblot analysis showed that in NIH3T3 cells, phosphorylation of IRSp53 S455 and afadin S1275 was substantially decreased upon expression of Phactr1XXX, and by serum stimulation, which activates rho-actin signalling and Phactr-family/PP1 complex formation (Miralles et al., 2003; Vartiainen et al., 2007; Wiezlak et al., 2012; Figure 3—figure supplement 1D; Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data.

claims.claim: Serum stimulation decreased phosphorylation of IRSp53 S455 and afadin S1275 in NIH3T3 cells.
claims.source: Immunoblot analysis showed that in NIH3T3 cells, phosphorylation of IRSp53 S455 and afadin S1275 was substantially decreased upon expression of Phactr1XXX, and by serum stimulation, which activates rho-actin signalling and Phactr-family/PP1 complex formation (Miralles et al., 2003; Vartiainen et al., 2007; Wiezlak et al., 2012; Figure 3—figure supplement 1D; Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data.

claims.claim: Treatment of NIH3T3 cells with cytochalasin D significantly decreased phosphorylation of IRSp53 S455 and afadin S1275.
claims.source: Moreover, treatment of cells with cytochalasin D (CD), which binds G-actin and disrupts its interaction with RPEL proteins (Vartiainen et al., 2007; Wiezlak et al., 2012) significantly decreased phosphorylation of IRSp53 S455 and afadin S1275 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E; Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data.

claims.claim: Treatment of NIH3T3 cells with latrunculin B increased phosphorylation of IRSp53 S455 and afadin S1275.
claims.source: In contrast, treatment of cells with the latrunculin B (LB), which increases G-actin concentration through blockade of F-actin assembly, but whose binding to G-actin does not affect RPEL-actin interaction, had the opposite effect (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E; Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data.

claims.claim: Phactr1 mutations are associated with morphological and functional developmental defects in cortical neurons.
claims.source: Phactr1 mutations are associated with morphological and functional developmental defects in cortical neurons (Hamada et al., 2018), and expression of Phactr1XXX induced morphological defects upon expression in cultured hippocampal neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hamada et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Expression of Phactr1XXX induced morphological defects in cultured hippocampal neurons.
claims.source: Phactr1 mutations are associated with morphological and functional developmental defects in cortical neurons (Hamada et al., 2018), and expression of Phactr1XXX induced morphological defects upon expression in cultured hippocampal neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: Phactr1-null mice are viable and do not show any obvious developmental abnormalities.
claims.source: Phactr1-null mice are viable; they do not show any obvious developmental abnormalities, and expression of the other Phactr proteins is apparently unaffected (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by observations of the Phactr1-null mice.

claims.claim: Expression of the other Phactr proteins is apparently unaffected in Phactr1-null mice.
claims.source: Phactr1-null mice are viable; they do not show any obvious developmental abnormalities, and expression of the other Phactr proteins is apparently unaffected (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: Among ~9000 phosphorylation sites quantified in the TMT phosphoproteomics experiment, 44 sites on 37 proteins differed significantly in their response to LB or CD stimuli in Phactr1-null cells.
claims.source: Among ~9000 phosphorylation sites quantified, we found 44 sites on 37 proteins that differed significantly in their response to these stimuli in Phactr1-null cells (Figure 3E, Supplementary file 1, Table E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by TMT phosphoproteomics data.

claims.claim: Seven phosphorylation sites, including IRSp53 pS455, spectrin αII pS1031, and afadin pS1275, were observed in both NIH3T3 cells and neurons.
claims.source: The sequence context of these sites was similar to that of those seen in NIH3T3 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C), and seven, including IRSp53 pS455, spectrin αII pS1031, and afadin pS1275, were observed in both cell types (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 2D; Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison of phosphoproteomics data from both cell types.

claims.claim: The structures of the IRSp53(449-465) and spectrin αII (1025–1039) complexes were determined at 1.09 Å and 1.30 Å resolution, respectively.
claims.source: This approach allowed determination of the structures of the IRSp53(449-465) and spectrin αII (1025–1039) complexes at 1.09 Å and 1.30 Å resolution, respectively (Figure 4A–C; Table 1; Figure 4—figure supplement 1; referred to hereafter as the IRSp53 and spectrin complexes), but was unsuccessful with Tbc1d15, Plekho2, afadin, and cofilin.
claims.evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data.

claims.claim: The Phactr1/PP1-IRSp53 and Phactr1/PP1-spectrin complexes crystallised in the same spacegroup.
claims.source: The Phactr1/PP1-IRSp53 and Phactr1/PP1-spectrin complexes crystallised in the same spacegroup.
claims.evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data.

claims.claim: Each asymmetric unit of the Phactr1/PP1-IRSp53 and Phactr1/PP1-spectrin complexes contains two complexes.
claims.source: Each asymmetric unit contains two complexes (RMSD 0.22 Å and 0.17 Å over 288 Cα, respectively), in which substrate-Phactr1/PP1 interactions are mostly conserved, albeit with some minor differences (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data.

claims.claim: The substrate sequences make extensive contacts across the PP1 catalytic site, then extend in a sinuous trajectory across the composite Phactr1/PP1 surface.
claims.source: The substrate sequences, whose N-termini are largely unresolved, make extensive contacts across the PP1 catalytic site, then extend in a sinuous trajectory across the composite Phactr1/PP1 surface, making numerous hydrophobic and ionic contacts (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by structural analysis of the crystal structures.

claims.claim: The complexes contain a presumed phosphate anion at the catalytic site and appear to represent putative enzyme/product complexes.
claims.source: Like the Phactr1/PP1 holoenzyme, the complexes contain a presumed phosphate anion at the catalytic site, and thus appear to represent putative enzyme/product complexes (see below).
claims.evidence: This is supported by structural analysis and inference.

claims.claim: The structure of Phactr1/PP1 in both substrate complexes is identical to that of the isolated Phactr1/PP1 complex.
claims.source: The structure of Phactr1/PP1 in both complexes is identical to that of the isolated Phactr1/PP1 complex (RMSD 0.31 Å over 313 Cα and 0.32 Å over 307 Cα, respectively).
claims.evidence: This is supported by structural comparison.

claims.claim: IRSp53 and spectrin make virtually identical contacts with the PP1 catalytic cleft, predominantly via their mainchains.
claims.source: IRSp53 and spectrin make virtually identical contacts with the PP1 catalytic cleft, predominantly via their mainchains (Figure 4C; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by structural analysis of the crystal structures.

claims.claim: The phosphate is inverted in the substrate complexes compared with the holoenzyme complex.
claims.source: The phosphate is inverted compared with the holoenzyme complex, losing its contact with PP1 R96 and H125, but making contact with the S455IRSp53/S1031spectrin hydroxyl (Figure 4D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by structural comparison.

claims.claim: The majority of the PP1 catalytic cleft residues that contact IRSp53 and spectrin are conserved among PPP family members, including PP5.
claims.source: The majority of the PP1 catalytic cleft residues that contact IRSp53 and spectrin are conserved among PPP family members, including PP5, which has been crystallised in complex with a phosphomimetic derivative of its substrate, Cdc37(S13E) (Oberoi et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by sequence conservation analysis and citation to Oberoi et al., 2016.

claims.claim: In the PP5/Cdc37(S13E) complex, PP5 residues corresponding to PP1 R96, H125, Y134, R221, and Y272 make contacts with Cdc37(S13E) analogous to those seen in the Phactr1/PP1-substrate complexes, despite Cdc37(S13E) docking in the opposite orientation.
claims.source: Strikingly, in that complex, the PP5 residues corresponding to PP1 R96, H125, Y134, R221, and Y272 make contacts with Cdc37(S13E) analogous to those seen in the Phactr1/PP1-substrate complexes, despite the fact that Cdc37(S13E) docks in the PP5 catalytic cleft in the opposite orientation to IRSp53 and spectrin (Figure 4—figure supplement 2; see Discussion).
claims.evidence: This is supported by structural comparison with the PP5/Cdc37(S13E) complex.

claims.claim: The phosphate in the Phactr1/PP1 holoenzyme structure is positioned similarly to the phosphorylated S455IRSp53/S1031spectrin of the bound substrate.
claims.source: It is generally accepted that the phosphate seen in many PPP family protein structures binds the active site in a similar way to the substrate phosphate (Egloff et al., 1995; Griffith et al., 1995; Mueller et al., 1993; Swingle et al., 2004), and we therefore assume that the phosphate in our Phactr1/PP1 holoenzyme structure is positioned similarly to the phosphorylated S455IRSp53/S1031spectrin of the bound substrate (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is based on established knowledge and inference from the structures.

claims.claim: In the PP5/Cdc37(S13E) complex, the phosphomimetic glutamate sidechain carbonyl is virtually superposable on the phosphate in the Phactr1/PP1 complex.
claims.source: Consistent with this idea, in the PP5/Cdc37(S13E) complex, the phosphomimetic glutamate sidechain carbonyl is virtually superposable on the phosphate in the Phactr1/PP1 complex (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by structural comparison.

claims.claim: The Phactr1/PP1 complex contains a bound water, W1, presumably activated by the metal ions and PP1 D64 and D92.
claims.source: The Phactr1/PP1 complex also contains a bound water, W1, presumably activated by the metal ions and PP1 D64 and D92 (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by structural analysis and inference about the catalytic mechanism.

claims.claim: W1 is oriented appropriately for in-line nucleophilic attack on the substrate phosphate.
claims.source: W1 is oriented appropriately for in-line nucleophilic attack on the substrate phosphate: this would be facilitated by protonation of the phosphoserine oxygen by the PP1 catalytic dyad H125-D95, and would result in inversion of the phosphate (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is based on structural analysis and inference about the catalytic mechanism.

claims.claim: The structures provide direct evidence for the in-line nucleophilic hydrolysis mechanism for PPP family phosphatases.
claims.source: The structures thus provide direct evidence for the in-line nucleophilic hydrolysis mechanism for PPP family phosphatases, as outlined by the Barford and Ciszak groups (Egloff et al., 1995; Swingle et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is based on structural analysis and comparison with proposed mechanisms.

claims.claim: The hydrophobic doublet L459-L460IRSp53/L1035-L1036spectrin (+4/+5) makes intimate contact with the Phactr1/PP1 hydrophobic pocket, entirely burying the +5 leucine sidechain.
claims.source: In both structures, the residues +3 to +6 form a β-turn, allowing the hydrophobic doublet L459-L460IRSp53/L1035-L1036spectrin (+4/+5) to make intimate contact with the Phactr1/PP1 hydrophobic pocket, entirely burying the +5 leucine sidechain (Figure 4C and F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by structural analysis of the crystal structures.

claims.claim: Alanine substitutions at positions S453 (−2), S454 (−1), and T456 (+1) in IRSp53 decreased catalytic efficiency somewhat, apparently reflecting an increased KM.
claims.source: Alanine substitutions at positions S453 (−2), S454 (−1), and T456 (+1) decreased catalytic efficiency somewhat, apparently reflecting an increased KM.
claims.evidence: This is supported by in vitro phosphatase assay data.

claims.claim: Alanine substitution of IRSp53 residues L459, L460, and D461 (+4 to +6) individually increased KM.
claims.source: In contrast, alanine substitution of residues L459, L460, and D461 (+4 to +6) individually increased KM, but had variable effects on catalytic efficiency, with L459A and D461A increasing it, and L460A reducing it (see Discussion).
claims.evidence: This is supported by in vitro phosphatase assay data.

claims.claim: The IRSp53 LL459/460AA mutant was essentially unreactive in the in vitro dephosphorylation assay.
claims.source: Pairwise combination of substitutions at positions +4 through +6 suppressed reactivity even more, with the LL459/460AA mutant being essentially unreactive.
claims.evidence: This is supported by in vitro phosphatase assay data.

claims.claim: IRSp53(L460A) exhibited enhanced basal phosphorylation and was less susceptible to CD-induced dephosphorylation than wildtype IRSp53 in NIH3T3 cells.
claims.source: Upon expression in NIH3T3 cells, IRSp53(L460A) exhibited enhanced basal phosphorylation, and was less susceptible to CD-induced dephosphorylation than wildtype IRSp53, as assessed using the phospho-S455 antibody (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data.

claims.claim: Substrate interactions with the Phactr1/PP1 hydrophobic pocket are important for efficient dephosphorylation both in vitro and in vivo.
claims.source: These data show that substrate interactions with the Phactr1/PP1 hydrophobic pocket are important for efficient dephosphorylation both in vitro and in vivo.
claims.evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis data from both in vitro assays and cell-based experiments.

claims.claim: Only peptides representing low KM substrates - IRSp53, spectrin αII, Tbc1d15 and Plekho2 - exhibited detectable binding in the peptide overlay assay.
claims.source: Only peptides representing low KMsubstrates - IRSp53, spectrin αII, Tbc1d15 and Plekho2 - exhibited detectable binding under the conditions of the assay (Figure 5—figure supplement 1; see Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by peptide overlay assay data.

claims.claim: Positions +4 and +5 in the substrate displayed the strongest selectivity in the peptide array, for hydrophobic residues and leucine respectively.
claims.source: Analysis of both arrays implicated residues −2 to +7 in substrate-binding affinity. Positions +4 and +5 displayed the strongest selectivity, for hydrophobic residues and leucine respectively: indeed, phenylalanine substitution of IRSp53 L459 (+4), increased binding affinity and catalytic efficiency (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by peptide array data.

claims.claim: Phenylalanine substitution of IRSp53 L459 (+4) increased binding affinity and catalytic efficiency.
claims.source: Positions +4 and +5 displayed the strongest selectivity, for hydrophobic residues and leucine respectively: indeed, phenylalanine substitution of IRSp53 L459 (+4), increased binding affinity and catalytic efficiency (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by peptide array and phosphatase assay data.

claims.claim: Interactions with the Phactr1/PP1 hydrophobic pocket are a critical determinant of Phactr1/PP1 substrate recognition.
claims.source: Taken together with the kinetics data, these results show that interactions with the Phactr1/PP1 hydrophobic pocket are a critical determinant of Phactr1/PP1 substrate recognition.
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence including structural, kinetic, and binding data.

claims.claim: In the Phactr1/PP1-IRSp53(S455E) complex, IRSp53 T456 occupies the position corresponding to S455 in the wildtype complex.
claims.source: Strikingly, in this complex, the phospomimetic glutamate (S455E) does not replace phosphate at the catalytic site. Instead, IRSp53 T456 occupies the position corresponding to S455 in the wildtype complex, with a recruited phosphate positioned as in the wild-type complex, and the glutamate (S455E) in effect occupies position −1, pointing away from the catalytic site (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by structural analysis of the Phactr1/PP1-IRSp53(S455E) complex.

results.result: PP1 phosphatases have little intrinsic sequence specificity, and while cofactors (PIPs) can target PP1 to substrates or locations and enhance/inhibit activity, no instances of PIP-induced sequence-specificity were known prior to this study.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C17, C18, and C19 establish the prior state of knowledge about PP1 specificity through citations to established literature (Brautigan and Shenolikar 2018; Miller and Turk 2018; Ichikawa et al. 1996; Johnson et al. 1996). This provides essential context for the novelty of the current work.

results.result: Phactr1 is a neuronally enriched PP1 cofactor controlled by G-actin through RPEL motifs, with G-actin competing with PP1 for binding due to overlap of the C-terminal RPEL domain with the PP1 binding sequence, allowing rho-actin signaling to control Phactr/PP1 complex formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C23-C28 describe established properties of Phactr proteins supported by multiple citations (Allen et al. 2004; Huet et al. 2013; Mouilleron et al. 2012; Wiezlak et al. 2012). This background information is well-documented in prior literature.

results.result: Phactr1 C-terminal sequences (517-580) containing the RVxF-like sequence LIRF are necessary and sufficient for PP1 binding with 10.4 nM affinity, comparable to other PIPs. Crystal structures of Phactr1/PP1 complexes were determined at 1.9-1.94 Å resolution, showing PP1 conformation virtually identical to other PP1 complexes.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C41 are supported by bio-layer interferometry data (C37-C38) and high-resolution crystallographic structures (C39-C41) with appropriate controls and comparisons to published structures. The binding affinity measurements and structural data are internally consistent and well-documented.

results.result: Phactr1 residues 516-542 wrap around PP1 in a manner similar to spinophilin, PNUTS, and PPP1R15B, with the RVxF sequence LIRF(519-522) being critical for binding. Systematic mutagenesis revealed quantitative contributions of individual residues to binding affinity, with deletion of LIRF reducing affinity ~10,000-fold and specific mutations reducing affinity 4-fold to >300-fold.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C53 are supported by structural analysis (C42-C43) and comprehensive mutagenesis data with BLI measurements (C44-C53). The mutagenesis is systematic and quantitative, with appropriate controls. The structural similarity to other PIPs is validated by RMSD calculations and citations.

results.result: Phactr1 binding remodels PP1's hydrophobic groove to create a novel composite surface comprising a deep hydrophobic pocket, an adjacent amphipathic cavity, and a basic rim, which radically alters PP1 surface charge distribution in a manner distinct from spinophilin/PP1.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C54-C67 are supported by high-resolution structural data showing detailed molecular interactions and surface properties. Mutagenesis data (C55-C59) validate the functional importance of the identified structural features. Electrostatic surface potential calculations and comparisons with spinophilin/PP1 support the claim of distinct remodeling.

results.result: SILAC phosphoproteomics in NIH3T3 cells identified over 3000 phosphorylation sites, with annotation enrichment analysis revealing that Phactr1/PP1 substrates are enriched in cytoskeletal components and regulators. Sites with high dephosphorylation scores showed enrichment of acidic residues at positions +2 to +7 and hydrophobic residues at +4/+5.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C73, C5 are supported by comprehensive SILAC phosphoproteomics data with appropriate controls (Phactr1XXX vs Phactr1XXXΔC and vector). Annotation enrichment analysis using established methods (Cox and Mann 2012) identified statistically significant GO categories. Sequence analysis revealed clear positional preferences.

results.result: In vitro phosphatase assays revealed that candidate substrates exhibit a range of kinetic parameters, with IRSp53 pS455 showing low KM and high kcat/KM. The four substrates with lowest KM (IRSp53 pS455, Plekho2 pS395, spectrin αII pS1031, Tbc1d15 pS205) all contained a leucine doublet at positions +4/+5.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C77 are supported by systematic in vitro phosphatase assays with quantitative kinetic measurements. The correlation between leucine doublets and low KM is based on direct observation across multiple substrates, though the mechanistic basis is explained by subsequent structural studies.

results.result: Phosphorylation of IRSp53 S455 and afadin S1275 was substantially decreased by Phactr1XXX expression and serum stimulation in NIH3T3 cells. Treatment with cytochalasin D (which disrupts G-actin-RPEL interaction) decreased phosphorylation, while latrunculin B (which increases G-actin but doesn't disrupt RPEL binding) increased phosphorylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C81 are supported by immunoblot data with phospho-specific antibodies and appropriate pharmacological controls. The opposing effects of CD and LB are consistent with the model that G-actin-Phactr binding regulates PP1 complex formation. Quantitation is provided in Supplementary file 3.

results.result: Phactr1-null mice are viable without obvious developmental abnormalities and with unaffected expression of other Phactr proteins. TMT phosphoproteomics in neurons identified 44 sites on 37 proteins that differed significantly in their response to CD/LB stimuli in Phactr1-null cells, with seven sites (including IRSp53 pS455, spectrin αII pS1031, afadin pS1275) observed in both NIH3T3 cells and neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C87 are supported by RT-PCR data (C85) and TMT phosphoproteomics with appropriate statistical analysis (C86). The overlap between cell types (C87) strengthens the identification of bona fide substrates. However, the viability of Phactr1-null mice (C84) suggests potential compensation by other Phactr family members.

results.result: High-resolution structures of Phactr1/PP1 bound to IRSp53(449-465) and spectrin αII(1025-1039) were determined at 1.09 Å and 1.30 Å resolution using PP1-substrate fusion proteins. The complexes contain phosphate at the catalytic site and appear to represent enzyme-product complexes, with substrate sequences making extensive contacts across the PP1 catalytic site and the composite Phactr1/PP1 surface.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C94 are supported by high-resolution crystallographic data with excellent statistics (Table 1). The fusion protein strategy is well-justified and analogous to published PP5 work (Oberoi et al. 2016). The structures show clear electron density for substrates and phosphate, supporting the enzyme-product complex interpretation.

results.result: The phosphate is inverted in substrate complexes compared to the holoenzyme, with a bound water (W1) positioned for in-line nucleophilic attack on the substrate phosphate. This inversion provides direct evidence for the in-line nucleophilic hydrolysis mechanism proposed for PPP family phosphatases.
results.evaluation: Claims C95, C7, C98-C102, C137 are supported by high-resolution structural data showing phosphate positions in both holoenzyme and product complexes. The interpretation is consistent with established mechanistic proposals (Egloff et al. 1995; Swingle et al. 2004) and comparison with the PP5/Cdc37(S13E) structure. This represents strong structural evidence for the catalytic mechanism.

results.result: Substrate sequences C-terminal to the dephosphorylation site make intimate contacts with the composite Phactr1/PP1 surface, with the hydrophobic doublet L459-L460 (IRSp53) or L1035-L1036 (spectrin) at positions +4/+5 making critical contacts with the hydrophobic pocket. Mutagenesis showed these interactions are required for efficient dephosphorylation both in vitro and in vivo.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C103-C108 are supported by structural data showing detailed substrate-enzyme contacts and systematic mutagenesis with both in vitro kinetic measurements and cellular validation. The LL459/460AA mutant being essentially unreactive (C106) and IRSp53(L460A) showing enhanced basal phosphorylation in cells (C107) provide strong functional validation.

results.result: Peptide overlay assays showed that only low KM substrates (IRSp53, spectrin αII, Tbc1d15, Plekho2) exhibited detectable binding. Peptide array analysis revealed that positions +4 and +5 displayed the strongest selectivity for hydrophobic residues and leucine, respectively, with phenylalanine substitution at IRSp53 L459 (+4) increasing both binding affinity and catalytic efficiency.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C112 are supported by peptide overlay assays and systematic peptide array data. The correlation between binding affinity and KM is logical, and the enhancement by F459 substitution (C111) provides functional validation. The comprehensive mutagenesis across all positions strengthens the conclusions about specificity determinants.

results.result: In the Phactr1/PP1-IRSp53(S455E) phosphomimetic complex, T456 occupies the position of S455 in the wildtype complex, with the glutamate at position -1. Critical contacts with the hydrophobic pocket are maintained. Both IRSp53 pT456 and E455/pT456 were effective substrates with only 2-fold lower catalytic efficiency, while pS453 and pS454 were very poor substrates, indicating that substrates can tolerate 3 or 4 residues between the target and the hydrophobic pocket.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C117 are supported by a 1.39 Å structure of the S455E complex and kinetic data for alternative phosphorylation sites. The structural observation that the substrate can shift register while maintaining pocket contacts (C113-C114) is directly validated by the kinetic data showing T456 is an effective substrate (C115). This demonstrates flexibility in the recognition mechanism.

results.result: Phactr1/PP1 exhibits 100-400-fold greater catalytic efficiency toward its substrates (IRSp53 pS455, CD2ap pS458, afadin pS1275) compared to apo-PP1 or spinophilin/PP1. However, cofilin pS3 showed only 2-fold enhancement. Phactr1 did not enhance activity against glycogen phosphorylase pS15 or GluR1 pS863. A PP1-Phactr1 fusion protein behaved similarly, indicating RVxF interactions are not essential for specificity.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C31, C34, C118-C122 are supported by comprehensive comparative phosphatase assays with multiple substrates and enzyme forms. The differential enhancement (100-400-fold for good substrates vs 2-fold for cofilin) and lack of activity against non-substrates demonstrates genuine sequence specificity. The fusion protein control (C121) validates that the composite surface, not just RVxF binding, confers specificity.

results.result: Efficient catalysis requires interactions between conserved hydrophobic residues in substrates and the novel Phactr1-PP1 composite surface (hydrophobic pocket, amphipathic cavity, basic rim). Phactr/PP1 substrates can be defined by a core recognition sequence S/T-x(2-3)-ϕ-L, with a hydrophobic doublet at +4/+5 or +3/+4 and leucine preferred at the distal position, embedded in acidic sequences. This is perhaps the first identified sequence specificity motif for PP1.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C33, C123, C144-C145 synthesize structural, kinetic, and binding data to define a consensus sequence. The proposal is well-supported by multiple lines of evidence: structural contacts, mutagenesis, peptide arrays, and kinetic measurements. The comparison to kinase recognition sequences (C145) is appropriate, though the claim of being 'the first' for PP1 should be qualified by the lack of prior systematic studies.

results.result: Phactr1/PP1 dephosphorylates multiple cytoskeletal proteins and regulators identified by phosphoproteomics. Substrates include IRSp53 (a Cdc42/Rac effector) at pS455 and pS367 (14-3-3 binding sites), spectrin αII and girdin at sites adjacent to SH3/SH2 domains, and the actin depolymerizing factors cofilin and destrin.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C130 are supported by phosphoproteomics data and citations to prior functional studies. The identification of specific sites (C127-C128) is validated by multiple approaches. The functional context provided by citations (Cohen et al. 2011; Kast and Dominguez 2019; Huet et al. 2013) strengthens the biological significance.

results.result: Phactr1 is enriched at the post-synaptic density and required for neuronal migration and arborization. Several Phactr1-dependent substrates (IRSp53, spectrin αII) are dephosphorylated during LTP, and IRSp53-null mice exhibit deficits in hippocampal learning and memory. Cofilin dephosphorylation is implicated in dendritic spine remodeling. In humans, Phactr1 mutations cause West syndrome.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C136 are supported by citations to published studies (Allen et al. 2004; Hamada et al. 2018; Li et al. 2016; Bobsin and Kreienkamp 2016; Kang et al. 2016; Bosch et al. 2014; Lei et al. 2017). These claims establish the neurobiological context and significance of the findings, though they represent prior work rather than new results from this study.

results.result: The majority of PP1 catalytic cleft residues contacting substrates are conserved among PPP family members including PP5. Surprisingly, Phactr1/PP1 substrates dock in the opposite orientation to that seen in the PP5/Cdc37(S13E) complex, despite analogous contacts by conserved residues.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C97, C138 are supported by structural comparisons with the PP5/Cdc37(S13E) structure (Oberoi et al. 2016) and sequence conservation analysis. The opposite orientation is clearly documented in Figure 4—figure supplement 2. This observation raises interesting questions about substrate recognition diversity in the PPP family.

results.result: The additional binding energy from substrate interactions with the hydrophobic pocket is proposed to be responsible for enhanced catalytic rate. Substrates with higher KM might be more promiscuous in their PP1 complex interactions (exemplified by cofilin pS3), while high binding affinities might limit catalytic efficiency by slowing product dissociation (possibly exemplified by spectrin).
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C142 represent mechanistic interpretations and speculations based on the kinetic data. While the general principle that binding energy enhances catalysis is sound (C139), the specific proposals about promiscuity (C140-C141) and product dissociation (C142) are speculative and would require additional experiments (e.g., product release measurements, competition assays) to validate.

results.result: Targeting the composite Phactr1/PP1 surface may be a good strategy for creating specific Phactr/PP1 inhibitors. Mutation of positions +4/+5 in candidate substrates will be useful for generating constitutively phosphorylated mutants for functional studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C143 and C146 represent reasonable proposals based on the findings. C143 is supported by the demonstration that the composite surface confers specificity and citation to the lack of specificity in current PP1 inhibitors (Zhang et al. 2013). C146 is validated by the demonstration that L460A mutation increases basal phosphorylation in cells (C107).

results.result: Spinophilin remodels the PP1 hydrophobic groove differently than Phactr1 and does not enhance PP1 activity toward Phactr/PP1 substrates. MYPT interacts with PP1 differently, extending both C-terminal and acidic grooves. PIPs constrain specificity by occluding PP1 surfaces. Phactr-family members lack conserved autonomous substrate-binding domains seen in other PIPs.
results.evaluation: Claims C147-C151 are supported by structural comparisons (C147, C149), biochemical data (C148), and sequence analysis (C151), all with appropriate citations. These comparisons contextualize the Phactr1/PP1 mechanism within the broader landscape of PP1 regulation and highlight its unique features.

results.result: Many PIPs target PP1 to specific subcellular locations. Phactr-family proteins exhibit differential subcellular localizations and Phactr1 interacts with the KCNT1 potassium channel. Membrane targeting involves conserved N-terminal sequences. The genetic dominance of Phactr mutations suggests interactions with other cellular components beyond PP1. The range of substrates controlled by Phactr1/PP1 will reflect cellular actin dynamics, subcellular localization, and direct sequence recognition.
results.evaluation: Claims C152-C157 are supported by citations to published work and represent reasonable integration of the findings with prior knowledge. C157 is a well-reasoned synthesis acknowledging that substrate specificity in cells depends on multiple factors beyond the intrinsic sequence recognition demonstrated here.

results.result: Expression of activated Phactr1 derivatives (Phactr1XXX or the PP1-binding domain alone) induces F-actin rearrangements in NIH3T3 fibroblasts and morphological defects in cultured hippocampal neurons. Phactr1 mutations are associated with morphological and functional developmental defects in cortical neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C69, C82-C83 are supported by citations to prior work (Wiezlak et al. 2012; Hamada et al. 2018) and data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and 3—figure supplement 2A. These observations establish the functional consequences of Phactr1/PP1 activity and provide biological context for the substrate identification studies.

results.result: The overlap of the RVxF motif with RPEL3 explains why G-actin competes with PP1 to bind Phactr1 and Phactr4, allowing Phactr1/PP1 complex formation to be controlled by fluctuations in actin dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claim C124 is supported by structural data showing the overlap (C48-C49) and citations to prior functional studies (Huet et al. 2013; Wiezlak et al. 2012). This represents an important mechanistic insight into how actin dynamics regulate Phactr1/PP1 activity, integrating structural and functional data.
